'''''Hypochaeris radicata''''', phonetically ''hy-poh-KAIR-iss rad-ee-KAY-tuh'',<ref name=NCSU /> is sometimes spelled ''Hypochoeris radicata'' and known as '''catsear''', '''flatweed''',<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.iewf.org/weedid/Hypochoeris_radicata.htm |title=Factsheet - ''Hypochoeris radicata'' |publisher=Iewf.org |access-date=2010-09-15}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.golfandsportsturf.com.au/article.asp?ArticleID=45 |title=Turf Weeds - The Dandelions |website=Golf and Sports Turf Magazine |publisher=Glenvale Publications |first=Kerry C |last=Harrington |access-date=2010-09-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100923203819/http://golfandsportsturf.com.au/article.asp?ArticleID=45 |archive-date=2010-09-23}}</ref> '''cat's-ear''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> '''hairy cat's ear''',<ref>{{PLANTS |id=HYRA3 |taxon=Hypochaeris radicata |access-date=15 May 2015}}</ref>{{r |WPL:2013|page=104}} or '''false [[Taraxacum|dandelion]]'''. It is a [[perennial plant|perennial]], low-lying edible [[herb]] often found in [[lawn]]s. ''H. radicata'' has been used for both food and medinicinal purposes.<ref name="POWO:2026" />

The plant is [[native plant|native]] to [[Europe]],<ref name=AFI>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=hypochaeris+radicata Altervista Flora Italiana, ''Hypochaeris radicata'' L.] includes photos and European distribution map</ref> but has also been [[introduced species|introduced]] to the [[Americas]],<ref>[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Hypochaeris%20radicata.png Biota of North America Program 2014 county distribution map]</ref><ref>Jørgensen, P. M., M. H. Nee & S. G. Beck. (eds.) 2014. Catálogo de las plantas vasculares de Bolivia, Monographs in systematic botany from the Missouri Botanical Garden 127(1–2): i–viii, 1–1744.</ref><ref>Luteyn, J. L. 1999. Páramos, a checklist of plant diversity, geographical distribution, and botanical literature. Memoirs of The New York Botanical Garden 84: viii–xv, 1–278.</ref> [[Japan]],<ref name="efloras">{{cite web |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=220006707 |title=Flora of China, ''Hypochaeris radicata'' Linnaeus, 1753. <big>假蒲公英猫儿菊</big> jia pu gong ying mao er ju (Hairy cat's ear) |access-date=13 July 2026 }}</ref> [[Australia]],<ref>[https://bie.ala.org.au/species/https://id.biodiversity.org.au/node/apni/2907368 Atlas of Living Australia,  ''Hypochaeris radicata'' L., Cat's Ear]</ref> and [[New Zealand]], where it can be an [[invasive species|invasive]] [[weed]]. It is listed as a harmful, [[noxious weed]] by the [[Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment|Korean Ministry of Environment]]<ref name=AJ:2021 >{{cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=M. |last2=Kim |first2=B.W. |last3=Song |first3=U. |title=Allelopathic potential of invasive ''Hypochaeris radicata'' weed on ''Brassica napus'' and ''Lactuca sativa'' |journal=Allelopathy Journal |date=July 2021 |volume=53 |issue=2 |page=Introduction |url=https://www.allelopathyjournal.com/cmsb/uploads/AJ_53_(2)_July,_2021_(231-242,30).pdf |access-date=17 July 2026 |publisher=International Allelopathy Foundation}}</ref>{{r |PMC10772109|}} and in the northwestern [[U.S. state]] of [[Washington (state)|Washington]].<ref name=nwcb>{{cite web |url=http://www.nwcb.wa.gov/weed_info/Written_findings/Hypochaeris_radicata.html |title=The Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board - Catsear |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070311181041/http://www.nwcb.wa.gov/weed_info/Written_findings/Hypochaeris_radicata.html |archive-date=2007-03-11 }}</ref>

== Botany ==

The [[leaf|leaves]], which may grow up to {{convert|8|in|cm|spell=in}} long, are lobed and covered in coarse hairs, forming a low-lying [[rosette (botany)|rosette]] around a central [[taproot]]. Forked stems carry bright yellow [[flower head]]s, and when mature these form seeds attached to windborne "parachutes". All parts of the plant exude a milky [[sap]] when cut.<ref name="efloras" />

Like other members of the ''Hypochaeris'' genus, its [[Pseudanthium|capitula's]] [[Asteraceae#Floral heads|ray florets]] cycle, opening during daylight for pollination or seed dispersal, then close by nightfall. Some contend the opening of catsear's capitula is triggered by at least one–hour of bright sunlight (Percival, 1950); others claim dull and cloudy daylight is sufficient (Salisbury, 1964). The capitula remain open for 3–7 hours a day based on weather; shorter times during warmer periods, longer when cool and cloudy. Its inflorescences remain closed during rainy conditions.<ref name=Fermanagh />

The perennial plants remain a basal rosette during their first year, flowering initiating in the second annum. Mature plants live up to 10 years, flowering from spring to fall, plants producing nominally 2,300, but as many as 6,000 seeds per year. Mowing (or grazing) stimulates growth of additional flower stems, doubling their count, increasing flower (and seed) production.{{ r |Nawrocki| }} Seed viability is limited, less than a year; moist soil and light are required for germination.<ref name=goert /><ref name="clemson">{{cite web |last1=Jordan |first1=Jackie |title=Weed of the Month – Common Cats-ear |url=https://hgic.clemson.edu/weed-of-the-month-common-cats-ear/ |website=hgic.clemson.edu |publisher=Clemson Cooperative Extension |access-date=8 July 2026 |date=2026}}</ref> Dispersed [[achene]] is supported and carried by its feathery [[Pappus (botany)|pappus]] with 95% of the seeds launched by a {{convert|43|km|mi|abbr=off|order=flip|sp=us}}/hr wind traveling at least {{convert|10|m|ft|order=flip|sp=us}} from the parent plant before ground-fall, some known to reach {{convert|100|m|ft|order=flip|sp=us}} (Soons et al. 2004).{{r |Nawrocki| }}

''H. radicata'' can also reproduce [[Vegetative reproduction|vegetatively]] via [[Perennation|perennating buds]] in multi-crowned plants. When stressed from heavy grazing or mowing, the rootstock crown produces additional tap-roots enabling vegetative spread.<ref name=Fermanagh /> The plant's ground level splitting, cloning, is presumably initiated by preferential growth conditions between the competing crown sections, e.g. a localized pest or disease, or an inferior [[Substrate (biology)|substratum]] (MacDonald and Cavers, 1974).{{r |Aarssen:1981|page=374 }}

The annual appearance of a second plant generation is common, observed in higher latitude [[biomes]], e.g. [[British Columbia]].<ref name=goert />{{r |Aarssen:1981|page=375 }}

=== Etymology and differences from dandelions ===
''Hypochaeris radicata's'' genus, ''Hypochaeris'' or ''Hypochoeris'', is derived from [[Ancient Greek|Greek]] {{Lang|grc|ὑπό}} 'under' and {{Lang|grc|χοῖρος}} for 'a young pig', being its preferred food source.<ref name="Aarssen:1981">{{cite journal |last1=Aarssen |first1=Lonnie W. |title=THE BIOLOGY OF CANADIAN WEEDS: 50. Hypochoeris radicata L. |journal=Canadian Journal of Plant Science |date=April 1981 |volume=61 |issue=2 |pages=365-381 |doi=10.4141/cjps81-051 |url=https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/epdf/10.4141/cjps81-051 |access-date=2 July 2026 |publisher=Canadian Science Publishing |location=Ottawa, Ontario, Canada}}</ref> Its species, ''radicata'', means "with large, conspicuous roots" in [[Latin]] (derived from {{Lang|la|radix}} 'root').<ref name="Fermanagh">{{cite web |last1=Forbes |first1=Ralph |title=''Hypochaeris radicata'' L., Cat's-ear |url=https://fermanagh.bsbi.org/hypochaeris-radicata-l |website=fermanagh.bsbi.org |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain & Ireland |access-date=8 August 2026 |location=St Albans, Hertfordshire, England}}</ref>

Catsear is also known as ''false dandelion'',<ref name="AH165" /> commonly mistaken for true '''dandelions''' (''[[Taraxacum]]''). Both carry similar flowers which form windborne seeds. However, catsear flowering stems are forked and solid, whereas dandelions possess unforked, hollow stems ([[Peduncle (botany)|peduncles]]). Both plants have a rosette of leaves and a central taproot. The leaves of dandelions are jagged in appearance, whereas those of catsear are more lobe-shaped and hairy. The plants have similar uses.

''H. radicata'' is also misidentified as '''autumn hawkbit''' (''[[Scorzoneroides autumnalis]]'') and '''smooth cat's ear''' (''[[Hypochaeris glabra]]'') due to similarity of their bright yellow flowers,{{r |Aarssen:1981|p=365 }} the higher density of short, stiff hairs on its leaves being a distinguishing characteristic.<ref name=Fermanagh />

==Distribution and habitat==
''H. radicata'' is native from Europe to [[Caucasus]], and in North Africa.<ref name="POWO:2026">{{cite web |title=''Hypochaeris radicata'' |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/225575-1 |website=powo.science.kew.org |publisher=Plants of the World Online. Facilitated by the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew. |access-date=4 July 2026 |date=4 July 2026}}</ref>  It has been introduced in S and SE Asia, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Pacific islands, S and SE Africa, and North and South America.<ref name=efloras /> Its range has been reported from [[Tasmania]], 42°S Lat., to [[Scandinavia]], near 63°N; at elevations from [[sea-level]] to {{convert|1676|m|ft|sp=us}} in Colorado{{r |Aarssen:1981| }}<ref name=Fermanagh /> and {{convert|4500|m|ft|sp=us}} in Columbia's [[Andes|Andean Mountain Range]].<ref name="POWO:2026" />

==Ecology==
''Hypochaeris radicata'' is considered a "nonhydrophyte" in the 2013 (US) National Wetland Plant List due to its preference for dryer upland soils. Dependent upon region, it may be found in wetlands, but not typically common.<ref name="WPL:2013">{{cite journal |last1=Lichvar |first1=Robert W. |editor1-last=Nesom |editor1-first=Guy L. |title=The National Wetland Plant List: 2013 wetland ratings |journal=Lilloa |date=17 July 2013 |url=http://www.phytoneuron.net/2013Phytoneuron/49PhytoN-2013NWPL.pdf |access-date=1 July 2026 |publisher=Phytoneuron |location=Fort Worth, Texas |pages=2,104 |issn=2153-733X |oclc=540632713}}</ref> Catsear can become a problematic weed, but does provide beneficial wildlife forage.<ref name="AH165">{{cite book |title=Index of Plant Diseases in the United States |date=Jan 1960 |publisher=Crops Research Division, Agricultural Research Service, U.S. Department of Agriculture |location=Washington, D.C. |page=80 |edition=Agriculture Handbook 165 |url=https://play.google.com/books/reader?id=ZYMWAAAAYAAJ&pg=GBS.PA80&hl=en |access-date=16 July 2026}}</ref>

===Pests and diseases===
 
*Parasites: Broomrape (''[[Orobanche minor]]''), a [[Obligate parasite|holoparasite]] plant, has invaded ''H. radicata'' in Canada{{r |Aarssen:1981|page=377 }} and the dense foliage of ''H. radicata's'' basal rosette is known to harbor [[slug#Feeding habits|slugs]], detrimental to other flora.{{r |Aarssen:1981|page=369 }}
*Insects and nematodes: ''H. radicata's'' ''[[asteraceae]]'' family is used as a food source by [[larva]]e of some ''[[lepidoptera]]'' species including the [[Shark (moth)|shark moth]], feeding on its flowers and leaves.<ref>{{cite web |title=Shark Moth, Cucullia umbratica |url=https://butterfly-conservation.org/moths/shark |website=butterfly-conservation.org |publisher=Butterfly Conservation |access-date=6 July 2026 |location=Dorset, England |date=2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260706173247/https://butterfly-conservation.org/moths/shark |archive-date=July 6, 2026}}</ref> ''H. radicata'' is known to be afflicted by soil-born stem nematodes (''[[ditylenchus dipsaci]]'');<ref name=AH165 /> gall midges (''[[contarinia|contarinia hypochoeridis]]''); [[gall wasp|cynipid wasps]]; and several weevils, e.g. the cribrate weevil (''[[otiorhynchus cribricollis]]'') and ''[[trachyphloeus scabriculus]]''.{{r |Aarssen:1981|page=377 }} 
*Fungi: Parasitic fungi include Hawkweed rust (''[[Puccinia|puccinia hieracii]]''), causing microscopic spore-producing pustules on leaf surfaces, leading to their curling, withering;<ref>{{cite web |title=''Puccinia Hieracii'' |url=https://plantiary.com/mushroom/puccinia-hieracii_130.html |website=plantiary.com |publisher=Plantiary |access-date=6 July 2026 |date=2025}}</ref><ref name=AH165 />{{r |Aarssen:1981|page=377 }} and [[Texas root rot|Phymatotrichum omnivorum]], a soil-born fungus causing root rot.<ref name=AH165 />
*Viruses: ''H. radicata'' is commonly affected by ''Hypochaeris'' [[Mosaic virus]] (HYMV00) in western Canada.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Hypochaeris mosaic'' virus (HYMV00) |url=https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/HYMV00 |website=gd.eppo.int |publisher=European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization (EPPO) |access-date=5 July 2026 |date=February 4, 2021}}</ref>{{r |Aarssen:1981|page=377 }}

===Ecological impact===
''H. radicata'' is a valuable plant for [[livestock]] and preferred by [[sheep]] and [[snowshoe hare]] over other food sources. Some have suggested its oversowing in grazed grasslands. Nutritionally, it is superior to many field grasses, comparable to [[Trifolium repens#Forage|white clover]]. Catsear's protein and mineral content measurably peak during spring and winter months.{{r |Aarssen:1981 }} It has invaded the semi-barren soil of over-grazed, abandoned pastures, beneficially increasing the volume of green leafy forage.<ref name=Fermanagh /> 

''H. radicata's'' ecological growth strategy is [[Plant strategies#Grime's C-S-R Triangle / Universal Adaptive Strategy Theory (UAST)|classified C-S-R]], Competitor, Stress-tolerator and [[Ruderal species|Ruderal]], a formidable, adversarial combination.<ref name=Fermanagh /> It can become a persistent weed in unwanted habitats. The species has invaded fragile ecosystems, habitat of rare and endangered plants. Its long leaves and dense rosette displace native annual species dependent upon accessible soil contact in open areas. It is classified as an invasive herbaceous weed in such locations.<ref name="goert">{{cite web |title=''Hypochaeris radicata''- Hairy Cat’s Ear |url=https://goert.ca/wp/wp-content/uploads/IS-factsheet-hypochaeris-radicata.pdf |website=goert.ca |publisher=Garry Oak Ecosystem Recovery Team |access-date=6 July 2026 |location=Vancouver Island, BC, Canada |date=2026}}
</ref> ''H. radicata's'' deep taproot draws and incorporates soil nitrogen, potentially reducing the residual nitrogen available for surrounding flora, stunting their growth.<ref name="Nawrocki">{{cite web |last1=Nawrocki |first1=Timm |title=hairy cat’s ear ''Hypochaeris radicata'' L. |url=https://accs.uaa.alaska.edu/wp-content/uploads/Hypochaeris_radicata_BIO_HYRA3.pdf |website=accs.uaa.alaska.edu |publisher=Alaska Natural Heritage Program, University of Alaska Anchorage |access-date=12 August 2026 |location=Anchorage, Alaska |date=8 December 2010}}</ref> During the 1980s, it was accidentally introduced onto [[Jeju Island]], a Korean [[Man and the Biosphere Programme#Biosphere reserves|Biosphere Reserve]], and within 3 decades had become the dominant invasive plant.<ref name=PMC10772109>{{cite journal |last1=Son |first1=Deokjoo |last2=Waldman |first2=Bruce |last3=Song |first3=Uhram |title=Effects of land-use types and the exotic species, Hypochaeris radicata, on plant diversity in human-transformed landscapes of the biosphere reserve, Jeju Island, Korea |journal=Plant Diversity |date=11 January 2023 |volume=45 |issue=6 |pages=685–693 |doi=10.1016/j.pld.2023.01.002 |pmid=38197002 |url=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10772109/ |access-date=11 August 2026 |pmc=10772109}}</ref> ''H. radicata'' seeds have been found as a contaminant in commercial seed products (Turkington and Aarssen 1983).{{r |Nawrocki| }} Evidence from ''H. radicata'<nowiki/>''s worldwide spread "strongly suggests" introduction via contamination of commercial crop and pasture seed mixes.<ref name=Fermanagh /> ''H. radicata'' is found on almost all continents (Ortiz et al. 2008).<ref name="ISMA" /> It has been introduced into at least 40 countries or islands, being classified "invasive" in six; Argentina, Brazil, Japan, Republic of Korea, Mexico and [[Réunion]];<ref name="gbif-cn" /><ref name=goert /><ref name=nwcb /> and as a "noxious specie" in Korea and Washington state.<ref name=AJ:2021 /><ref name=nwcb />

Its prolific reproduction and deep roots enable aggressive growth in lawns, newly plowed fields, and commercial berry fields.{{r |Aarssen:1981 }} It spreads by seed and if disturbed, by [[Root cap|crown]] and root [[Cutting (plant)|cuttings]].<ref name=nwcb /> Catsear successfully competes with other grassland species and is known to displace/destroy pasture lands within a 3-year period, even displacing preferred ''Trifolium repens'' (White Clover) stands. When applicable, it responds to common herbicides with the most effective outcome during the perennial's first growth year, its rosette stage, preceding flowering and dispersal.<ref name=goert /><ref name=Fermanagh /> ''H. radicata'' is effectively controlled by plowing and cultivation.

== Culinary uses ==
All parts of the catsear plant are edible; however, the leaves and roots are those most often harvested. The leaves are bland in taste but can be eaten raw in salads, steamed, or used in stir-fries. Some recommend mixing them with other vegetables.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Nyerges|first=Christopher|title=Foraging Washington: Finding, Identifying, and Preparing Edible Wild Foods|publisher=Falcon Guides|year=2017|isbn=978-1-4930-2534-3|location=Guilford, CT|oclc=965922681}}</ref> Older leaves can become tough and fibrous, but younger leaves are suitable for consumption. In contrast to the edible leaves of dandelion, catsear leaves only rarely have some bitterness. In [[Crete]], Greece, the leaves of a variety called {{lang|el|παχιές}} (''pachiés'') or {{lang|el|αγριοράδικα}} (''agriorádika'') are eaten boiled or steamed.<ref>{{cite book |author= Kleonikos G. Stavridakis, Κλεόνικος Γ. Σταυριδάκης  |title= Wild edible plants of Crete - {{lang|el|Η Άγρια βρώσιμη χλωρίδα της Κρήτης}} |publisher= Rethymnon Crete |year=2006 |isbn=960-631-179-1}}</ref>

The root can be roasted and ground to form a [[coffee]] substitute.

== Toxicity ==
This species is associated with [[stringhalt]] in horses and donkeys if consumed in excess, the exact etiology unknown;<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.seven.eques.com.au/health-pdf/Stringhalt.pdf |title=Australian stringhalt |author=John Kohnke |publisher=South East Victoria Equine Network |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110221204206/http://www.seven.eques.com.au/health-pdf/Stringhalt.pdf |archive-date=2011-02-21}}</ref><ref name="Merck">{{cite web |last1=Brokken |first1=Matthew T. |last2=Rice |first2=Hilary |title=Stringhalt |url=https://www.merckvetmanual.com/musculoskeletal-system/tendon-and-ligament-disorders-in-horses/stringhalt |website=www.merckvetmanual.com |publisher=Merck & Co., Inc. |access-date=8 July 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260708194548/https://www.merckvetmanual.com/musculoskeletal-system/tendon-and-ligament-disorders-in-horses/stringhalt |archive-date=July 8, 2026 |location=Rahway, NJ |date=October 2025}}</ref> otherwise non-poisonous and no [[contact dermatitis]] association.<ref name="NCSU" />
